title: Verification of death and care after death
blurb: Verify an expected adult death correctly, give dignified personal care after death and know when the coroner must be involved.
question: Mr Danso, 78, dies peacefully in a hospice at 21:05 after a documented DNACPR discussion. The registered nurse completes verification at 21:40. What does she record as the time of death, and what must she check before he is moved?

teach.body: Anyone can recognise that a person has died. Verification is the formal process of confirming and documenting the fact of death; competent registered nurses may verify an expected adult death. Certification (the medical certificate of cause of death) is separate and done by a doctor. In plain English: the nurse confirms that death has happened; the doctor says why.
teach.cite: Hospice UK, Care after death: RN verification of expected adult death (RNVoEAD), 6th ed., version 6.2 (2025)

teach.h: When can a registered nurse verify?
teach.note: A nurse found someone dead without a DNACPR record may still verify if there are signs of irreversible death such as rigor mortis. The nurse may refuse and request the doctor, or police if anything is unusual.

head: Check
Standard
rows: At least 5 minutes for irreversible arrest
No response to light, both eyes
None to trapezius squeeze after 5 min
teach.caption: Any spontaneous return of cardiac or respiratory activity during observation prompts a further 5 minutes of observation.

items.label: verify within this in the community

teach.caption: The time verification is completed is the official time of death; families should be told it will differ from the time of the last breath.

items: Lay the person on their back with limbs straight before rigor mortis (2–6 hours), one pillow under the head.
Close the eyes with light pressure for 30 seconds; do not tape them.
Do not bind the jaw with bandages, and do not shave the face.
Wash the person unless asked not to for religious or cultural reasons, or because of coroner involvement.
Warn colleagues that air may escape from the lungs when the person is moved.
Offer all key contacts the chance to view the person; respect spiritual, religious and cultural wishes.

teach.h: Lines and tubes: what stays in?

root.label: Is the death referred to the coroner?

teach.body: Refer when the cause of death is unknown; there is no attending practitioner; death may be due to violence, trauma or injury, poisoning, self-harm, neglect or failure of care, a medical procedure or treatment, or employment; or the person died in custody or state detention. A notifiable infectious disease is not, on its own, a reason to refer. The nurse must also tell mortuary staff or the funeral director about any infection risk, implants and whether an ICD is still active, and instigate ICD deactivation.
teach.cite: RNVoEAD 6th ed. (version 6.2) Appendix 1; Hospice UK Care after death 5.2

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Danso in the hospice
teach.body: Mr Danso, 78, dies at 21:05. Nurse Grace observes him for 5 minutes, confirms no central pulse or heart sounds for at least a minute each, no breathing, fixed pupils and no response to trapezius squeeze. She records 21:40, when verification is completed, as the official time of death and explains the difference to his wife. His death is expected and not suspicious, so no coroner referral is needed. She notes his pacemaker for the funeral director and supports the family's wish to wash him with her.

teach.text: Don't record the time of the last breath as the official time of death when a nurse verifies: it is the time verification is completed. And don't confuse 'notifiable disease' with 'coroner referral': a notifiable infection must be communicated to the mortuary and funeral director, but it is not a reason to refer to the coroner.

items: RN verification: adults over 18, expected, not suspicious; nurse may refuse and call a doctor or police.
Observe at least 5 minutes; pulse and heart sounds absent at least 1 minute; pupils fixed; no response to trapezius squeeze.
Official time of death = time verification completed. Verify within 1 h (hospital) or 4 h (community).
Personal care within 2–4 h; eyes closed with light pressure 30 s; no jaw binding or shaving.
Suspicious referral: leave everything, do not wash. Cause-of-death referral: leave lines and ET tube, spigot catheters.
Tell mortuary and funeral director about infection, implants and active ICDs.

summary: You can now verify an expected adult death to the RNVoEAD standard, record the official time of death and decide whether the coroner must be involved. You can also give personal care after death that protects dignity, evidence and the safety of others.

A.q: When verifying an expected adult death, for at least how long must the registered nurse observe the person to establish irreversible cardiorespiratory arrest?
options: 1 minute
2 minutes
5 minutes
10 minutes
A.why: RNVoEAD: observe for a minimum of 5 minutes; a further 5 minutes if any spontaneous return of activity is seen.

whyNot.0: One minute is the minimum for checking absence of a central pulse and heart sounds, not the whole observation.
whyNot.1: Two minutes is shorter than the national standard.
whyNot.3: Ten minutes is not the standard minimum, although it may follow if activity returns.

A.q: A community nurse completes verification of Mrs Iqbal's expected death at 04:25. Her husband says she took her last breath at 03:50. What is recorded as the official time of death?
options: The time the GP certifies
A.why: RNVoEAD 6.2: the time of verification is recognised as the official time of death; families should be told there will be a difference from the time of the last breath.

whyNot.0: The time of the last breath is meaningful to the family but is not the official time of death recorded by the verifier.
whyNot.1: There is no rounding of the official time.
whyNot.3: Certification of cause of death is a separate, later process.

A.q: During personal care after death, the nurse notices the person's eyes are partly open. What is the recommended action?
options: Hold the lids closed with a strip of clear adhesive tape
Place damp gauze pads over both eyes until rigor sets in
Leave them open for the funeral director to close
Apply light pressure to the lids for about 30 seconds
A.why: Hospice UK Care after death 5.2: close the eyes by applying light pressure for 30 seconds, which also protects tissue for possible corneal donation.

whyNot.0: Tape can mark the delicate skin of the eyelids and is not recommended.
whyNot.1: Damp gauze is not the recommended method in current guidance.
whyNot.2: Eyes should be closed as part of personal care, within the 2–4 hour window.

B.q: Kenneth, 70, dies on a surgical ward the day after an elective operation. There are no suspicious circumstances, but the death will be referred to the coroner. What should the nurse do with his cannula and urinary catheter?
options: Remove both and dispose of them as clinical waste
Leave the cannula in and spigot the catheter
Remove the cannula and leave the catheter bag full
Leave both and avoid any washing or personal care
B.why: Hospice UK 5.2 para 55: for a cause-of-death coroner referral without suspicion, leave IV cannulae and lines in situ and spigot catheters; personal care can then be given.

whyNot.0: Removing devices may hinder the coroner's investigation of a death related to a procedure.
whyNot.2: The cannula stays; catheter bag contents can be discarded per policy and the catheter spigotted.
whyNot.3: Avoiding all washing applies when there are suspicious circumstances; here personal care can be given.

B.q: Which death is a reason in itself for referral to the coroner?
options: An expected death from a notifiable infection
An expected death of a person with an active ICD
A death that may result from a medical procedure
A death that occurred unwitnessed during the night
B.why: RNVoEAD Appendix 1: deaths that may be related to a medical procedure or treatment require coroner referral.

whyNot.0: A notifiable infectious disease is not a reason to refer to the coroner.
whyNot.1: An ICD must be deactivated and the funeral director told, but it does not trigger coroner referral.
whyNot.3: An expected death at night, even if no one was present, does not on its own meet the referral criteria.

B.q: Mrs Fenwick, 84, has died in a care home and her death has been verified. She had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator that is still active. What must the registered nurse do?
options: Instigate deactivation and tell the funeral director
Remove the device before the body is moved
Refer the death to the coroner because of the device
Record it in the notes and take no further action
B.why: RNVoEAD: the RN must instigate deactivation of an ICD and notify the mortuary or funeral director of implants and whether an ICD is still active.

whyNot.1: Nurses do not remove implanted devices; deactivation is arranged and the funeral director informed.
whyNot.2: An implanted device is not a reason for coroner referral.
whyNot.3: An active ICD poses a risk to those handling the body, so action is needed.

C.q: A nurse arrives to verify the expected death of Mr Ali, 66, at home. His adult son says, 'He fell down the stairs this morning and seemed confused afterwards.' The nurse sees bruising to the head. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Verify the death, as it was expected from his cancer
Decline to verify and request the doctor or police
Verify the death and ask the GP to certify it
Wash the body before the family see him
C.why: RNVoEAD applies to expected deaths without suspicious circumstances. A fall with head injury means death may be due to trauma, which needs coroner referral; the nurse may refuse to verify and request the doctor or police.

whyNot.0: An expected diagnosis does not remove the possibility that trauma caused or contributed to death.
whyNot.2: Certification by the GP would bypass the coroner when injury may be involved.
whyNot.3: Washing could destroy evidence where a coroner referral is likely.

C.q: Mrs Rahman, 77, has died an expected death on a medical ward. Her family explain that, in keeping with their faith, they wish to bury her as soon as possible. The death is not being referred to the coroner. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat urgent release as time critical and involve chaplaincy
Explain release cannot occur until the usual 3 to 5 days
Refer to the coroner to obtain a faster release
Advise the family to arrange a private post-mortem examination
C.why: Hospice UK 5.2: urgent release for burial or cremation is time critical; seek spiritual care or chaplaincy advice and complete documentation promptly.

whyNot.1: There is no fixed waiting period; services should work to meet urgent release where possible.
whyNot.2: Referring an expected death that does not meet criteria is inappropriate and would slow release.
whyNot.3: A post-mortem is not needed and would delay burial.

C.q: A death on a ward is being referred to the coroner because staff suspect an unexplained injury. What should happen to the person's lines, tubes and personal care?
options: Remove lines, then wash and dress the person
Leave the ET tube and remove other lines
Wash the person but leave the catheter bag
Leave all lines and tubes in and do not wash
C.why: Hospice UK 5.2 para 54: in forensic referrals, minimal contact; leave all drains, tubes, cannulae and lines, clamp infusions, leave catheter and bag, and do not wash or begin mouth care.

whyNot.0: Removing lines and washing could destroy evidence.
whyNot.1: All lines and tubes stay, not just the ET tube.
whyNot.2: Washing is avoided in suspicious circumstances.

reteach.title: Verify, care, tell
reteach.question: After an expected death, what are the nurse's three jobs?

blocks.body: VERIFY: 5 minutes of observation and the RNVoEAD checks; record the time verification is completed. CARE: personal care within 2–4 hours that protects dignity, respects faith and culture, and preserves evidence if the coroner is involved. TELL: the doctor, the family (including the time difference), and the mortuary or funeral director about infection, implants and ICDs.

blocks.text: Verification is not certification. The nurse verifies the fact of death; a doctor certifies the cause.

explain.body: Competent RNs may verify expected deaths of adults over 18 with no suspicious circumstances. Verify within 1 hour in hospital and 4 hours in the community. The nurse may refuse and request the doctor, or police if unusual.

test.q: Within what time should an expected death in a hospital be verified, according to RNVoEAD?
options: 30 minutes
1 hour
4 hours
12 hours
test.why: RNVoEAD: timely verification is within one hour in hospital and within four hours in the community.

whyNot.0: Thirty minutes is not the stated standard.
whyNot.2: Four hours is the community standard.
whyNot.3: Twelve hours is far longer than either standard.

explain.body: Observe at least 5 minutes. No central pulse for at least 1 minute; no heart sounds for at least 1 minute; no respiratory effort; no pupillary response to light; after 5 minutes, no motor response to trapezius squeeze. Any return: observe 5 more minutes.

test.q: After five minutes of continued cardiorespiratory arrest, which test confirms absence of motor response?
options: Trapezius squeeze
Plantar reflex
Sternal rub for 2 minutes
Glasgow Coma Scale
test.why: RNVoEAD: after five minutes, confirm absence of motor response with the trapezius squeeze (supraorbital pressure is an alternative).

whyNot.1: The plantar reflex is a neurological examination sign, not the verification test.
whyNot.2: A sternal rub is not the RNVoEAD test.
whyNot.3: GCS is used in living patients to assess consciousness, not to verify death.

explain.body: Within 2–4 hours. Lie flat, limbs straight before rigor (2–6 h). Close eyes with light pressure 30 s. No jaw binding, no shaving. Wash unless faith, culture or the coroner say otherwise. Offer viewing to all key contacts.

test.q: A healthcare assistant starts to shave a man's face during care after death. What should the nurse advise?
options: Shave with an electric razor to avoid any nicks
Shave if the family will not be viewing him
Apply moisturiser first, then shave gently
Do not shave, as marks can appear days later
test.why: Hospice UK 5.2: do not shave the deceased person; shaving after death causes marking that may only appear days later.

whyNot.0: An electric razor still causes post-mortem marking.
whyNot.1: Whether the family view him does not change the advice; marking affects the funeral director's preparation too.
whyNot.2: Moisturiser does not prevent the marking.

explain.body: Refer if cause unknown, no attending practitioner, violence or injury, poisoning, self-harm, neglect, medical procedure, employment, custody or state detention. A notifiable disease alone is not a reason. Tell the mortuary or funeral director about infection, implants and active ICDs.

test.q: A patient has died of an expected death and had confirmed tuberculosis, a notifiable disease. What should the nurse do?
options: Refer the death to the coroner for review
Tell the mortuary or funeral director
Delay verification for 24 hours
Ask the family not to view the body
test.why: RNVoEAD: a notifiable infectious disease is not a reason to refer to the coroner, but infection risk must be communicated to mortuary staff and funeral directors.

whyNot.0: Notifiable infection alone does not meet coroner referral criteria.
whyNot.2: Verification should be timely, not delayed.
whyNot.3: Viewing should be offered; infection control measures are used as needed.
